Part 1: nephrosclerosis, secondary hypertension, renal artery stenosis, and Bartter/Gitelman/Liddle. Part 2: thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP, HUS) and the vasculitides. Tags: beyond source = added by me, not in his materials.

1. Nephrosclerosis: Arterial vs Arteriolar

  • Nephrosclerosis = scarring of the kidney from an underlying vascular condition. Two forms, depending on which vessel is diseased.
Arterial nephrosclerosisArteriolar nephrosclerosis (arteriolonephrosclerosis)
MechanismAtherosclerotic complication (emboli from a plaque, stenosis, thrombosis) → infarct → scarGeneralized thickening of the arterioles → low-level, diffuse ischemic injury
CauseAtherosclerosis (hypertension is a major risk factor for it)Hypertension or diabetes
GrossWell-defined, variably sized scars (loss of cortex, thinned cortex) with normal cortex in betweenDiffuse granularity of the cortical surface ("gravel road"); affects the whole kidney
MicroscopicFibrosis, globally sclerotic glomeruli, tubular atrophy, chronic inflammation (nonspecific)Same chronic changes plus hyaline arteriolosclerosis
How to picture the granularityEach affected arteriole produces a tiny micro-infarct at the cortical surface. Thousands of them give the roughened surface. Each little indentation corresponds to a patch of globally sclerotic glomeruli, scarring and tubular atrophy.

Arterial nephrosclerosis (scars from infarcts)

Slide: arterial nephrosclerosis. Arrows mark scars. The lower specimen is a remote infarct; because it sits at a pole, chronic pyelonephritis could look the same.
Slide: acute renal infarct. Hemorrhage and congestion around coagulative necrosis; a fibrin thrombus in the vessel caused the ischemia. If the patient survives, the dead cortex heals as a scar like the one above.
  • An acute infarct is coagulative necrosis from a thrombus or embolus. The cortex dies and later leaves a depressed scar.
  • Gross trap: a scar at a pole can be a remote infarct or chronic pyelonephritis (which classically involves the poles). Dr. Kemp finds these hard to tell apart.

Arteriolar nephrosclerosis (diffuse granularity)

Slide: diffuse granularity of the cortical surface, with the microscopic indentations that match it.
Slide: sclerotic glomeruli, fibrosis, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
Slide: hyaline arteriolosclerosis. This appearance is found in both hypertension and diabetes.
  • Hyaline arteriolosclerosis = pink, acellular, glassy thickening of the arteriolar wall that narrows the lumen.
  • Hypertension: pressure forces plasma proteins to leak into the wall.
  • Diabetes: advanced glycosylation end products accumulate in the wall.
  • Both end up with the same picture, so the histology alone cannot tell you which one the patient has.
Which arteriole? (his question, his understanding)On a glomerulus where you see both vessels: diabetes involves both afferent and efferent arterioles (the glycosylation products are present before and after the glomerulus), while hypertension involves only the afferent, because the blood pressure differs on the two sides. Dr. Kemp frames this as what he was taught, not a slide point.

Both together, and chronic kidney disease

Slide: arterial and arteriolar nephrosclerosis. Yellow arrows = cortical scars (arterial). Blue arrows = granular surface in between (arteriolar). Cut section: dilated pelvis and thinned cortex.
Slide: features of chronic kidney disease: globally sclerotic glomeruli (black arrows) and tubular atrophy with fibrosis (yellow arrow).
Slide: comparison. Top, arteriolar nephrosclerosis: fine granularity over the whole surface. Bottom, arterial nephrosclerosis: one depressed scar with smooth cortex around it.
  • Because hypertension drives atherosclerosis, the two forms commonly coexist: scars plus granular cortex between them.
  • Much of the parenchyma is lost, so the pelvis looks dilated and the cortex thin. The pictured kidney could also have a hydronephrosis component, but chronic pyelonephritis does not cause a granular cortical surface.
  • Chronic kidney disease look: globally sclerotic glomeruli (whole glomerulus scarred), tubular atrophy (wider spaces between tubules), fibrosis (confirm with a trichrome stain), scattered chronic inflammation.

2. Other Vascular Disease

  • Atheroembolic disease: a plaque ruptures and showers cholesterol emboli into the kidney. The classic microscopic sign is a needle-shaped cleft left in the vessel where the cholesterol crystal dissolved during processing.
  • Other emboli: fat, air, or projectiles (he has seen shotgun pellets in a kidney).
  • Diffuse cortical necrosis: if the main renal artery is blocked, the entire kidney is deprived of blood and the whole cortex dies. Gross: pale yellow discoloration of the cortex everywhere.
Slide: cholesterol embolus (arrow) in a kidney vessel.
Slide: diffuse cortical necrosis. Pale yellow cortex at every yellow arrow is ischemic injury.
Scale of the problemSmall branch occluded → wedge infarct and scar (arterial nephrosclerosis). Whole renal artery occluded → diffuse cortical necrosis.

3. Hypertension and the Kidney

Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)

Slide: role of the kidney in blood pressure.
  • Triggers for renin release by the juxtaglomerular cells: low arteriolar blood pressure, elevated catecholamines, low sodium at the distal convoluted tubule.
  • Renin converts angiotensinogen → angiotensin I; angiotensin I → angiotensin II.
  • Angiotensin II: contracts smooth muscle (vasoconstriction, higher pressure) and stimulates aldosterone.
  • Aldosterone: ↑ sodium resorption in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting tubule, ↑ potassium excretion. Water follows sodium, so blood volume and pressure rise.
  • So an aldosterone-secreting tumor gives high sodium (or high-normal) and low potassium plus hypertension.

Renal secondary causes of hypertension

Dr. Kemp: secondary causes make great test questions (unusual clinical settings), and in practice a few percent of "hypertension" is treatable, so find it and you can cure it.

CauseWhy it raises blood pressure
Acute glomerulonephritis (nephritic syndrome)Hypertension is a feature of the nephritic syndrome
Chronic renal diseaseRAAS activation; inability to control sodium and water
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney diseaseChronic kidney disease mechanism; also cyst compression ischemia beyond source
Renin-producing tumorsDirectly secrete renin, or paraneoplastic effect
Renal artery stenosisFibromuscular dysplasia or atherosclerotic disease (next section)

4. Renal Artery Stenosis and Fibromuscular Dysplasia

Two forms of renal artery stenosis:

Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)Atherosclerotic
WhoYoung females most commonly (but all ages and both sexes)People with atherosclerosis risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, older age, male
PathologyMedial fibroplasia (60–70%). Also perimedial fibroplasia, medial hyperplasia, intimal fibroplasia, adventitial fibroplasiaOrdinary plaque in the renal artery, often at the origin beyond source
Imaging"String of beads": alternating stenosis and aneurysmal dilationFocal narrowing
ComplicationsSecondary hypertension; rarely thrombosis (intimal type); dissectionSecondary hypertension
Clue wordsYoung woman + hypertension resistant to treatment + bilateral stenosis with intervening aneurysmal dilations = fibromuscular dysplasia. Whenever hypertension is resistant, think of a secondary cause.

Point to ponder: unilateral renal artery stenosis

Say the right renal artery is narrowed.

Stenotic kidney (right)Contralateral kidney (left)
PerfusionGets less blood than normalNormal flow, but exposed to high systemic pressure
SizeSmall, atrophicNormal size
SurfaceSmooth cortical surfaceGranular surface from hyaline arteriolosclerosis
RoleThinks the body is hypotensive → activates RAAS → raises systemic pressureSuffers the hypertension the other kidney caused
  • Dr. Kemp's logic: the body would rather be hypertensive than hypotensive (you can survive hypertension longer), so the stenotic kidney controls the body's pressure. The pressure it sets is too high for the other side.

5. Bartter, Gitelman and Liddle Syndromes

Hereditary tubular transport defects. These are Dr. Kemp's own diagrams. The objective is the mechanism; he promised there will be no exam question on them, but the mechanism explains each electrolyte pattern.

BartterGitelmanLiddle
Defect (slide)Sodium resorption lost in the thick ascending limb (Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ carrier)Sodium resorption lost in the distal convoluted tubule (Na⁺-Cl⁻); also affects the magnesium transporterGain of function of the sodium transporter in the collecting duct (the one aldosterone acts on)
Sodium and waterSodium stays in urine, water follows → volume loss → RAAS onSame: volume loss → RAAS on↑ sodium absorption, water retained → hypertension
PotassiumLoss: no K⁺ back-leak (beyond source classically hypokalemia)Hypokalemia beyond source↑ K⁺ excretion → hypokalemia
CalciumK⁺ does not recycle, so no lumen-positive drive for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ → hypercalciuriaCalcium resorption not tied to sodium → hypocalciuria—
MagnesiumHypomagnesemiaHypomagnesemia—
AldosteroneHigh (RAAS on)High (RAAS on)Low: the transporter works on its own, independent of aldosterone
Blood pressureNot hypertensive (volume loss) beyond sourceNot hypertensive beyond sourceHypertension
Stone riskYes (calcium in urine)No (hypocalciuria)—
Slide: Bartter syndrome. Red = primary mechanism, yellow = secondary effects.
Slide: Gitelman syndrome.
Slide: Liddle syndrome. Gain-of-function sodium transporter, aldosterone low.
Pattern to keepLose sodium upstream (Bartter, Gitelman) → volume depletion, high renin and aldosterone. Gain sodium (Liddle) → hypertension with suppressed renin and aldosterone (beyond source: a "pseudo-hyperaldosteronism"). Where the defect sits decides the calcium: Bartter (loop-like) wastes calcium; Gitelman (thiazide-like) retains it. beyond source

6. Thrombotic Microangiopathies (TMA)

  • Thrombotic microangiopathy = disease of small vessels (arterioles, venules, capillaries) with tiny thrombi forming throughout.
  • Versus disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): the microscopy looks the same, but in DIC clotting factors are used up, so PT and PTT are abnormal. In TMA PT and PTT are normal; the platelets are low.

Types

GroupExamples
PrimaryTTP and HUS
HUS, typical (D+)Diarrhea-associated: E. coli, Shigella, Pseudomonas (slide list)
HUS, atypical (D−)Mutation in, or autoantibodies against, factor H (also C3 and other complement factors that control C3 convertase)
SecondaryDrugs (mitomycin, cisplatin, cyclosporine); autoimmune (SLE, scleroderma); malignant hypertension (onion-skinning arterioles); pregnancy and postpartum

Clinical pentad

  1. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: red cells fragment as they streak past the little clots, forming schistocytes.
  2. Thrombocytopenia
  3. Fever
  4. CNS changes (more common in TTP), e.g., mental status changes
  5. Renal disease (more common in HUS)

Patients do not need all five. Typical HUS has a sudden onset after a GI or flu-like illness.

TTPHUS
DefectADAMTS13: inherited defect, or antibodies (autoimmune or drug-induced)Sporadic (D+): Shiga toxin (glomerular endothelial cells have its receptor); adults: Shiga-like toxin. Atypical (D−): complement factors (factor H)
ResultLarge von Willebrand factor (VWF) multimers activate platelet aggregation → small-vessel thrombosisPlatelet activation and aggregation → small-vessel thrombosis
Leans towardCNS changesKidney disease
Slide (autopsy case of TTP): microthrombus in an arteriole of cardiac muscle (arrow). Dr. Kemp found them in the vessels supplying the atrioventricular node and suspected arrhythmia from ischemia as the cause of death.
Slide: silver stain, thrombi in glomerular capillary loops. The kidney is a great place to look for microthrombi.
Slide question: HUS17-year-old, fever, pallor, oliguria, petechiae (eyes and mouth), low hemoglobin and platelets, high BUN and creatinine, ate raw beef at a cookout → hemolytic uremic syndrome. Petechiae = thrombocytopenia; low hemoglobin = microangiopathic hemolytic anemia; BUN and creatinine = renal injury; raw beef = Shiga toxin-producing E. coli beyond source.

7. Vasculitis: Concepts and ANCA

  • Vasculitis = inflammation of the vessel wall.
  • Pathologic findings can be nonspecific (granulomas and transmural necrosis occur in several). Clinical findings are broad but usually include fever, myalgia, arthralgia, malaise. Diagnosis needs the combination.
  • Each disease favors one vessel size, but there is overlap (polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-vessel disease that can involve smaller or larger vessels). Large = aorta and big muscular arteries; medium = muscular arteries; small = arterioles, capillaries, venules.
  • Vessel inflammation can lead to thrombosis, stenosis, aneurysm and infarction.
  • Differential rule: any systemic illness involving many organs may be a vasculitis.

General clinical scenarios

  • Fever and weight loss; multi-organ involvement
  • Renal involvement (hematuria and proteinuria)
  • Arthralgia and myalgia with skin rash or nasal crusting and epistaxis
  • Eye inflammation with systemic symptoms
  • Atypical pneumonia with fever, weight loss, arthralgia or myalgia

Not all of these apply to every vasculitis.

ANCA (anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody)

  • p-ANCA = perinuclear staining on indirect immunofluorescence; target myeloperoxidase (MPO) → MPO-ANCA; linked to microscopic polyangiitis.
  • c-ANCA = cytoplasmic staining; target proteinase 3 → PR3-ANCA; linked to granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener).
  • These autoantibodies directly activate neutrophils (reactive oxygen species and enzyme release cause damage). Now tested by ELISA.
Diseasec-ANCA (PR3)p-ANCA (MPO)
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis66%24%
Microscopic polyangiitis26%58%
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis<5%40%

Source on slide: Bakerman, ABC's of Interpretive Laboratory Data, 5th ed.

  • Other ANCA-positive conditions: lupus, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, IgA nephropathy, TTP, infections, neoplasms.
  • Not absolutely specific for any one disease, just part of the overall diagnosis.
Mnemonic warningDr. Kemp admits his own mnemonic for the p/c split did not work and he retracted it. Use the facts: p = perinuclear = MPO (microscopic polyangiitis); c = cytoplasmic = PR3 (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, "c" for classic Wegener).

8. The Vasculitides and the Kidney

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)

  • Symptoms/signs variable: commonly kidneys, heart, skeletal muscle, skin, mesentery, but any organ.
  • Temporally heterogeneous: lesions are of different ages (acute fibrinoid necrosis next to healed scar).
  • Segmental fibrinoid necrosis (smudgy pink wall) with transmural inflammation; healing leaves fibrosis of the media and breaks in the elastic lamina.
  • Not associated with ANCA. Hepatitis B association.
  • Lung involvement was once thought rare, but a 1993 study (Matsumoto) showed pulmonary complications are not rare.
Slide: polyarteritis nodosa. Lumen nearly obliterated; fibrinoid necrosis and transmural inflammation.
Slide: segmental nature. Fibrinoid necrosis on the left; the vessel looks intact on the right (hence pathologists cut many sections of a temporal artery biopsy).

Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA)

  • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: proteinuria, hematuria, RBC casts; hypertension.
  • Pulmonary capillaritis: hemoptysis, infiltrates, effusions, edema, pleuritis (looks like Goodpasture, but no linear immunofluorescence).
  • Skin (purpura), nerves (peripheral neuropathy), GI tract (abdominal pain, bleeding).
  • Lab: p-ANCA (MPO) in 50–75%.
  • Pathology: necrotizing vasculitis like PAN, but all lesions are the same age.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA, Wegener)

  • c-ANCA (PR3). Males > females, around 40 years.
  • Classic triad: upper respiratory (sinusitis, perforated nasal septum), lower respiratory (pneumonitis), kidney (hematuria, proteinuria). Also rash and musculoskeletal.
  • Pathology: acute inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis; chronic vessel inflammation with medial thickening and intimal proliferation; necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomas; glomerular disease from focal necrotizing to crescentic glomerulonephritis (rapidly progressive).
  • Dr. Kemp has rarely been able to identify true granulomas in biopsies. Expect a stem with the classic three sites plus c-ANCA.
Slide: granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Lung with patchy inflammation; glomerulus with a crescent (cellular proliferation) compressing the capillary tuft.
Slide: crescent in a glomerulus, close up. The crescent surrounds and pushes the capillary tuft aside.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, Churg-Strauss)

  • Rare (1–3 per million). p-ANCA in a minority.
  • Associated with asthma and eosinophilia (the clinical hook).
  • Affects lungs, spleen, kidney, heart, liver, CNS. Fibrinoid necrosis → thrombosis and aneurysms; granulomas and eosinophilic infiltrates.

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura)

  • 90% in childhood. Related to IgA nephropathy, but here the vessels are involved.
  • Purpura (often lower extremities), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain (GI bleeding possible), renal disease.
  • Pathology: leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits.
